headline: Sanofi Lines Up Takeover Target to Fix Pharma’s Lowest Valuation
author: Margaryta Kirakosian

paragraphs.text: (Bloomberg) -- To understand why Sanofi is pursuing what would be the biggest takeover in the pharmaceutical industry in years, look no further than one number.

Even after a surge since early October, the stock trades at 9 times estimated earnings, making Sanofi the cheapest among the world's 10 biggest pharmaceutical companies by sales. The multiple is below the group average of 17.3. The stock is underperforming many of its big rivals this year.

Investors aren't willing to pay up for Sanofi because — while it's posting booming sales now of its skin and asthma drug Dupixent — they can see the dreaded patent cliff coming. Dupixent will begin to lose patent protection in 2031, and skeptics aren't convinced the company has the experimental treatments in its pipeline to replace the revenue.

That leaves the option of acquiring promising drugs: Sanofi is considering an acquisition of US drugmaker Insmed Inc., people familiar with the matter said this week. The company has a market value of $31.6 billion and has two approved drugs for respiratory diseases on the market.

"Bold moves rarely come without risks, and it might be the right time for Sanofi's management to take some calculated chances," Abhishek Raval, an analyst at Alphavalue in Paris, said by email. Buying Insmed "would certainly be a massive step in answering the market's pressing question around Sanofi's life after Dupixent."

Both companies have declined to comment on a potential deal, which would be the biggest in the industry since Pfizer Inc. bought Seagen Inc. for $43 billion in late 2023. Sanofi shares fell 2.9% Thursday on the report, though they pared some of that drop on Friday.
Chief Executive Officer Belén Garijo has made it clear she knows investors are looking ahead.

"The whole organization is focused on managing Sanofi's post-Dupixent trajectory over the next decade," she said in the company's earnings statement last month. "Our priority is to protect earnings through Dupixent's loss of exclusivity." Sanofi raised its full-year sales and profit forecasts for a second straight quarter on strong demand for Dupixent.
Garijo took charge of Sanofi this year after previously working at Merck KGaA, and investors are still assessing her ability to pull off the kind of acquisition Sanofi may need.

The company probably can afford to spend more than €25 billion ($27.5 billion) without jeopardizing the dividend or its credit rating, analyst Michael Leuchten at Jefferies said in a note Thursday, and the Insmed deal might be within reach.

"A sizeable M&A transaction should provide greater stability through the Dupixent patent cliff and, hence, create time for Sanofi to reload its pipeline," he wrote. "Bottom line for us is that whilst this looks big on paper, it is doable, digestible and directionally seems consistent with what management was aiming for."
Sanofi shares, meanwhile, have returned 8.9% this year including reinvested dividends, underperforming the 11% return for the Stoxx Europe 600 Health Care Index.

Even before the Insmed report, some analysts were arguing the market was pricing in the Dupixent problem too early and giving Sanofi too little credit for the cash the drug can generate before the patent expiration. Intron Health's Naresh Chouhan raised the stock to buy from hold this month and set the highest price target among analysts tracked by Bloomberg, implying a 41% gain from current levels.
Some of that thesis is already playing out. The shares have surged 12% since Sanofi's better-than-expected earnings and higher forecast on Oct. 30.

Chouhan expects Dupixent sales to jump to €34 billion in 2031 from €15.7 billion last year. He's also upbeat about its M&A prospects. These are among key factors behind his call that Sanofi will be the best EU pharma stock by the end of 2027.

BNP Paribas analyst Peter Verdult upgraded the shares to outperform this month, arguing that concerns over the weak pipeline are already reflected in the valuation, while investors underestimate Dupixent's near-term earnings potential.
